summaries.gardner: AbbVie is a large incumbent in a mature industry, so it does not fit Gardner's Rule Breaker profile of a top dog in an emerging industry. It has a sustainable edge in next-generation immunology (Skyrizi and Rinvoq, about $26B of 2025 sales) and decent momentum (+19% over 52 weeks), but the AbbVie name itself is little known and the stock is rarely called overvalued on forward earnings.
summaries.buffett: AbbVie offers an understandable franchise with strong free cash flow ($17.8 billion in 2025) and 54 years of dividend growth counting its Abbott history. Buffett-style concerns are the reliance on patents that expire, a debt-heavy balance sheet ($70.8 billion of debt, negative equity) built through acquisitions, and GAAP earnings ($2.36 per share in 2025) far below cash earnings, which makes owner earnings harder to judge.
summaries.munger: Munger would respect the skill shown in replacing Humira with Skyrizi and Rinvoq, but inverting shows several ways to lose: patent cliffs, US drug-price regulation (IRA negotiation already hit Imbruvica), heavy debt and serial acquisitions. At about 18 times forward earnings the price is fair rather than a bargain.
summaries.lynch: AbbVie is a Lynch stalwart with a simple story: Skyrizi and Rinvoq growth plus new launches should lift revenue about 10% in 2026 to roughly $67.6 billion. Its PEG of about 1.35, negligible insider buying and heavy Wall Street coverage mean it does not pass Lynch's bargain and neglect tests.
summaries.fisher: AbbVie fits Fisher's points on sales strength and on developing new products as old ones mature, having rebuilt growth after Humira's US biosimilar loss in 2023. Its R&D productivity is mixed (emraclidine failed in 2024) and much innovation is bought rather than discovered, while GAAP operating margins have fallen from 31.9% in 2021 to 24.6% in 2025.
summaries.graham: AbbVie passes Graham's size, dividend-record and continuous-profit tests but fails the defensive investor's financial-strength and price tests. Book equity is negative, the current ratio is about 0.8, and the stock trades at about 78 times trailing GAAP earnings.
summaries.thiel: AbbVie is not a zero-to-one company: its moats are patents and commercial reach, not technology ten times better than rivals. It has strong distribution and a big share of IL-23 immunology, but its durability depends on continually replacing drugs before patents expire.
summaries.gerstner: Gerstner would like the visible growth (2026 revenue guided about 10% higher) and strong free cash flow, but AbbVie is not tied to the AI platform shift he focuses on. At about 18 times forward earnings and a 3.8% free-cash-flow yield it looks reasonably priced, with the main debates being Medicare price negotiation and pipeline returns from acquisitions.
summaries.druckenmiller: From Druckenmiller's angle, AbbVie offers steady upward guidance revisions (2026 revenue guidance raised by $600 million year to date) and catalysts such as tavapadon and Rinvoq label expansions. It is a low-beta defensive stock (5-year beta about 0.2) rather than a liquidity-driven, accelerating-earnings story he would size big.
summaries.smith: Terry Smith would like the high gross margins (about 70% GAAP, above 84% adjusted) and strong cash conversion, but would question the reliance on acquisitions, heavy leverage and the payout ratio of nearly 200% of GAAP earnings. ROIC around 18% is good but supported by debt, so it only partly fits his 'good company' tests.
summaries.greenblatt: On Greenblatt's Magic Formula, AbbVie has a good return on capital (about 18% ROIC) but a modest earnings yield, with operating profit of about $22.9 billion against an enterprise value of about $549 billion (around 4%). That combination would not rank it near the top of a Magic Formula screen.
summaries.akre: Akre's three legs are only partly met: the business is good (high margins, strong cash flow), management has executed well through the Humira cliff, but reinvestment is mostly through costly acquisitions rather than high-return internal compounding.
summaries.pabrai: AbbVie is not a Dhandho-style bet: there is no deep distress or obvious mispricing, and with a value of about $103 per share in a conservative 12% DCF against a price near $275, the downside is not clearly protected. The business is resilient, but the margin of safety Pabrai demands is absent.
summaries.wood: AbbVie does not fit Cathie Wood's disruptive-innovation focus: it is not a leader in AI, multiomic sequencing or another ARK platform, and its growth is steady rather than exponential. Its antibody-drug conjugates and Parkinson's launches are innovative but incremental.
summaries.ackman: AbbVie partly fits Ackman's criteria of a simple, predictable, cash-generative business with barriers to entry, but its debt load, patent-expiry risk and regulatory exposure reduce predictability. There is no obvious activist catalyst.
summaries.sleep: Nick Sleep's 'scale economics shared' model does not apply: AbbVie captures rather than shares its scale benefits, pricing its drugs high while patents last. Its position in 10 to 20 years depends on drugs not yet approved.
summaries.valentine: Valentine looked for huge markets and technologies solving painful problems; AbbVie's immunology and neuroscience drugs do solve painful problems, but it is a mature incumbent, not an early-stage company riding a new technology wave.
summaries.nash: AbbVie scores about 70 on Nash's 13 categories, short of 75: it has a large business with 24.6% GAAP operating margin and low short interest, but carries far more debt than cash ($70.8 billion vs $6.6 billion), which is one of his instant kills. Revenue growth around 9-10% and a DCF value well below the share price also fall short of his tests.

momentum.evidence: ABBV rose 19.0% over the 52 weeks to 13 October 2026 (close $274.36 per StockAnalysis), roughly in line with the S&P 500 rather than clearly beating it.

g4.evidence: Management executed the Humira transition well and 76.6% of shares are held by institutions, but there is no famous anchor investor or visionary leader.

g6.evidence: At about 18 times forward earnings and an average analyst target ($282.61) near the price, it is generally called fairly valued rather than overvalued.

simple.evidence: It sells prescription medicines and Botox; the key drivers (Skyrizi, Rinvoq, patent expiries) are easy for a generalist to follow.

b2.evidence: Revenue grew from $45,804M in 2020 to $61,160M in 2025 and the dividend has risen every year since the 2013 spin-off, but GAAP earnings fell from $11,836M in 2022 to $4,226M in 2025.

integrity.evidence: Disclosure and guidance are clear and guidance has been raised in 2026, but the Humira patent thicket and high leverage from deals draw criticism.

b6.evidence: Deals like Allergan (2020), ImmunoGen, Cerevel and Apogee (about $10.9B) broaden the pipeline but show a strong reliance on acquisitions.

roic.evidence: ROIC is about 17.7% (StockAnalysis), but the company runs with $70.8B of debt and negative book equity.

fcf.evidence: Free cash flow was $17,816M in 2025 against GAAP net income of $4,226M, as acquired R&D and amortization are non-cash or one-off.

b10.evidence: Retained earnings and borrowings funded acquisitions that rebuilt revenue after Humira, but market cap gains have come with a much larger debt load.

safety.evidence: A conservative 12% DCF gives about $103 per share versus a price near $275, so there is no margin of safety.

fairprice.evidence: About 18 times forward earnings and a 3.8% free-cash-flow yield is reasonable for ~10% guided revenue growth, but not cheap.

mu5.evidence: The business is diversified across immunology, neuroscience, oncology and aesthetics, but patent cliffs, drug-price laws and debt are real failure paths.

reinvest.evidence: It can reinvest in R&D (about $9.8B adjusted in 2026) and deals, but returns on acquisitions are uncertain.

ly2.evidence: It is a stalwart: a large drugmaker growing about 10% a year on Skyrizi and Rinvoq.

ly3.evidence: The forward P/E of about 18 is above the expected earnings growth rate, with a PEG of about 1.35.

runway.evidence: Skyrizi and Rinvoq still add new indications and Parkinson's/ADC launches add growth, but consensus sees revenue growth slowing to mid-single digits by 2030 (about $83.8B).

ly7.evidence: Insiders own about 0.07% with no notable open-market buying found, and the share count was roughly flat (+0.03%) over the past year.

ly8.evidence: AbbVie is a widely followed megacap covered by about 30 analysts.

fi2.evidence: It built Skyrizi and Rinvoq into successors to Humira and is launching Vyalev, tavapadon and antibody-drug conjugates.

fi3.evidence: R&D delivered Skyrizi and Rinvoq, but notable failures include emraclidine in schizophrenia (2024), and many assets come from acquisitions.

fi4.evidence: Its commercial machine drove Skyrizi from launch to $17,562M of 2025 sales, guided to $21.7B in 2026.

longterm.evidence: It invests about $9.8B a year in adjusted R&D, but also prioritises a high dividend and near-term EPS guidance.

gr1.evidence: Revenue was $61,160M in 2025 and market value is about $485B.

ni10.evidence: AbbVie has reported positive GAAP net earnings every year since its 2013 spin-off, including $4,226M in 2025.

gr4.evidence: AbbVie itself has paid dividends only since 2013, though counting Abbott's record it has 54 years of dividend growth; the annual rate is $6.92.

eps10.evidence: GAAP diluted EPS of $2.36 in 2025 is below the 2020 level of $2.72 and far below 2022's $6.63.

gr6.evidence: The trailing GAAP P/E is about 78, far above 15.

gr7.evidence: Book equity is negative (-$5,935M at June 2026), so P/E times P/B cannot meet the test.

th1.evidence: Its drugs are better than older therapies but not ten times better than rivals' IL-23, IL-17 or JAK drugs.

timing.evidence: Immunology demand keeps growing and Humira's erosion is largely behind it, but IRA negotiation is starting to bite.

th3.evidence: It began as Abbott's pharma arm with Humira already a blockbuster, not with a small niche.

team.evidence: CEO Rob Michael (since 2024) is a capable operator from finance, not an exceptional founder.

th5.evidence: Its large sales forces, payer contracting and direct-to-consumer advertising are a major distribution advantage.

durable.evidence: Immunology leadership should hold into the 2030s, but drug patents expire, so 20-year durability depends on future products.

trend.evidence: It benefits from aging populations and rising treatment of immune diseases, but is not a platform-shift beneficiary like AI.

dr2.evidence: Humira's drag shrinks and launches add growth, but IRA price cuts and the Apogee deal dilution offset part of that.

dr4.evidence: It is defensive and insensitive to the economy, but high debt makes interest rates matter (2026 net interest guided about $2.9B).

gm.evidence: GAAP gross margin was 70.2% in 2025 and adjusted gross margin is guided above 84% for 2026.
